title: TCS Opens India's First Lights-Out Factory Lab in Pune for AI Manufacturing
excerpt: The Industrial Autonomy & Engineering Lab features a fully robotic battery pack assembly line where manufacturers can prototype AI-first production systems before deploying them in real factories.
body:
• Tata Consultancy Services on September 9, 2026, launched the TCS Industrial Autonomy & Engineering Lab – Lights-Out Factory at its Sahyadri Park campus in Pune, which it describes as India's first lights-out factory lab for AI-led manufacturing.
  • A lights-out factory is one where autonomous systems run production lines with minimal human intervention; the Pune lab houses a fully robotic battery pack assembly line as a live multi-stage demonstration environment.
  • The facility combines digital twins, robotics, industrial AI, factory control systems, and real-time operational intelligence, letting manufacturers prototype, validate, and scale AI-first production systems before deploying them in real factories.
  • The launch extends TCS's industrial-AI footprint — earlier this year it opened a Physical AI lab in Bengaluru with NVIDIA — and reflects the company's stated goal of becoming the world's largest AI-powered technology services company.

Tata Consultancy Services has opened what it describes as India's first "lights-out" factory laboratory — a manufacturing facility where autonomous systems run production with minimal human intervention. Announced September 9 through a regulatory filing, the TCS Industrial Autonomy & Engineering Lab – Lights-Out Factory sits at the company's Sahyadri Park campus in Pune and is built to advance AI-led manufacturing for industrial customers.

The centerpiece is a fully robotic battery pack assembly line. The live, multi-stage setup lets manufacturers prototype, validate, and scale AI-first production systems while reducing the deployment risks of putting unproven automation into real factories, the company said.

What the lab actually does

The facility simulates how self-optimizing factories can automate workflows by combining five technology pillars: digital twins, robotics, industrial AI, factory control systems, and real-time operational intelligence. In practice, the lab supports industrial use cases including predictive maintenance, automated quality inspection, real-time process optimization, human-machine collaboration, and autonomous factory operations.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=-fgslWv810U

TCS framed the lab around a specific pain point its clients face: translating Industry 4.0, AI, and robotics concepts into practical operating models. The Pune facility gives manufacturers a controlled setting to explore industrial scenarios, assess their suitability for production environments, and de-risk the investment before committing to a full rollout. The operating philosophy is what TCS calls its Human+AI Service Autonomy Model — the idea that enterprises move from digitally enabled operations toward increasingly autonomous production systems, with humans and AI systems collaborating rather than the latter simply replacing the former.

"We have built a facility that can help customers turn their aspiration of lights-out manufacturing into a reality. The lab provides a tangible demonstration of how the Human + AI model can help enterprises progress from digitally enabled operations to increasingly autonomous production systems."

— Sreenivasa Chakravarti, Global Head & Vice President of Industrial Autonomy and Engineering, TCS

"When we think of a manufacturing facility, we picture legacy factories and heavy equipment, that run on intense manual effort," Chakravarti added. "At TCS, we are reimagining those environments and building factories for the future."

Part of a bigger Physical AI push

The Pune lab is the latest addition to TCS's industrial autonomy and engineering footprint. Earlier this year, the company launched the TCS Industrial Autonomy & Engineering Lab Powered by NVIDIA in Bengaluru, aimed at accelerating "Physical AI" — AI systems that operate in the physical world — for industrial and mobility applications. Taken together, the two labs signal a strategic shift for the IT services giant: from pure-play software integration toward building physical laboratories that simulate industrial environments and give clients a place to test robotics, vision AI, and digital twins in live manufacturing settings.

The bet fits the company's stated goal: "to become the world's largest AI-powered technology services company, enabling customers to transform across the entire AI value chain, from infrastructure to intelligence." Recent wins, like a five-year, €1.25 billion deal with Porsche to industrialize AI across its engineering and operations, show the industrial-autonomy pitch landing with automotive clients.

Customer interest is already visible. Joakim Landholm, SVP for commercial and operations development at industrial group SKF, said the next phase of manufacturing will require smarter, more energy-efficient, and more reliable operations, and that the TCS lab could help industries apply advanced automation and industrial AI to achieve measurable operational improvements.

What it means — and what to watch

The timing suits India's manufacturing ambitions: battery pack assembly, the lab's showcase application, sits at the heart of the EV transition, where precision and repeatability decide margins.

What to watch next: whether the Pune lab converts demonstrations into signed industrial contracts, how TCS prices and packages its Human+AI services for mid-size manufacturers (not just automotive giants), and whether competitors in the IT services industry answer with their own physical labs. The facility is a bet that the future of industrial IT is not just software delivered remotely — it is AI embedded in machines on the factory floor.
